newsitem.title: ANGOLA: U.N. announces wind-down of Angolan peacekeeping.
newsitem.headline: U.N. announces wind-down of Angolan peacekeeping.

text.p: The United Nations announced on Thursday it would begin to wind down its 6,500-man peacekeeping operation in Angola from December, signalling the start of a new era for the southern African country.
If all goes well, troops from Zimbabwe, Brazil, India, Portugal, Romania, South Korea and Uruguay will have packed up and left for home by February 1997, a senior U.N. official told Reuters.

In less than two years, after the first deployment of a multi-national peacekeeping force in Angola, the U.N. has helped to end Africa's longest and one of its bloodiest civil wars between the government and rebel UNITA forces.

The director of the U.N.'s African peacekeeping division, Hedi Annabi, told Reuters significant progress had been made in implementing the 1994 Lusaka peace protocol and both sides appeared to be cooperating. It was therefore no longer necessary to maintain the full mission, he said.
"We will begin downsizing the peacekeeping operation from the end of December with the withdrawal of four companies of soldiers because some of the tasks have been completed," Annabi said.
At a cost of $1 million a day, the U.N. Security Council has over recent months shown impatience with the two factions in their implementation of the peace pact.

Annabi said the U.N. could no longer afford to keep troops in Angola and a downscaling was necessary with the pullout of the first four companies -- about 600 troops -- at the end of December, ahead of a larger withdrawal in February.
"We don't want to unnecessarily keep troops here...It is expensive.

"Facts show that progress has been made, although it has been slow and is behind schedule. We hope that both parties will have completed their tasks by February. There is not much need for peacekeepers if those parties are cooperating," Annabi said.
The peacekeepers have not only helped to maintain a ceasefire but have also helped to rebuild roads and bridges to free landlocked communities.
The opening of roads through government and UNITA controlled areas have also given aid agencies access to thousands of starving Angolans, who were dying at a rate of 300 a day two years ago.

One of the biggest achievements of the peacekeeping mission has been the disarming of UNITA's guerrilla force of more than 63,000 men, assembling them in 15 camps around the country ahead of demobilisation.
It has also helped to collect the rebels' war materials and in many areas secure roads for the free movement of people.

Also on Thursday, a joint peace commission comprising the two Angolan factions plus observer states and the U.N. declared it was satisfied the government and UNITA had substantially complied with military tasks set out in the peace pact.

The U.N. Special Envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, told a news conference: "The delegation unanimously concluded with great satisfaction that tasks set out by the Security Council have been completed...some 100 percent, others 80 percent, and others 75 percent."
From now on the commission would dedicate its time to implementing a political timetable which foresees a unity government, Beye said.
